opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that 80% is both encouraging and nowhere near good enough. It's encouraging because a few years ago, if you'd asked whether a robot foundation model could reason about the semantic safety of an instruction at all, whether "put the cup on the stove" is fine but "put the plastic container on the hot burner" isn't, or whether handing scissors blade-first to a child is a problem, the answer would have been basically no. These models are now picking up a lot of common-sense physical and social safety knowledge from the language and vision pretraining. That's real progress.

But you have to put 80% in context. In robotics, the bar isn't "right most of the time." If a robot is in your home doing hundreds of actions a day, a one-in-five failure rate on safety-relevant judgments is completely unacceptable. We expect safety-critical systems to have many nines of reliability. So I see that number as a measure of how far we have to go, not a sign that we're close.

It's also important to be clear about what a benchmark like that measures. A lot of it tests semantic safety: does the model understand that a situation or instruction is dangerous, and can it decline or flag it? That's a different layer from low-level physical safety, like collision avoidance, force limits, and not crushing someone's hand. Those classical safeguards still matter a lot and should stay in the stack. What the foundation models add is the ability to reason about the long tail of situations nobody wrote a rule for. That's exactly where you need them, and exactly where they're least reliable.

So the way I think about it is in layers. You want a constitution or a set of principles the model is trained and evaluated against. You want the model to be able to critique its own plans before executing them. And you want hard constraints underneath that don't depend on the model getting the reasoning right. No single layer will get you to the reliability you need, but stacked together they can get much closer.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that benchmarks need to keep evolving. Once a number like 80% gets published, people optimize for it, and the risk is we saturate the benchmark without actually making robots safer in the real world. So we need data grounded in real injury reports and real failure modes, adversarial testing, and eventually evaluation in physical deployment, not just question-answering about images. We're still early, and I think the right attitude is cautious optimism with a lot of humility.

r002.rationale: It says robot-model safety is still early, but does not compare its maturity with language-model safety.

r003.rationale: It describes the benchmark as testing semantic safety and distinguishes that from low-level physical safety, so 80% does not represent overall robot safety.

r004.rationale: It says classical safeguards should stay in the stack and that hard constraints should remain underneath the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest way to put it is that 80% sounds decent until you remember what the task actually is. If you're a robot operating in someone's kitchen, or around a child, or near a stove, getting the safety call right four out of five times is not a passing grade. That's not a product. That's a liability.

And I want to be careful about what that number is measuring, because it's easy to over-read it. Asimov is largely a judgment benchmark. We're asking the model, often in a text or image-plus-text setting, "is this action acceptable, is this situation dangerous, what would a reasonable person do here." So the 80% is really telling you about the model's semantic understanding of safety constraints. It's about whether the model knows the rule. It is not telling you whether the robot will actually honor that rule when it's executing a low-level policy at 50 hertz with a gripper in motion. Those are two different problems, and I think people conflate them constantly.

So on the first problem, the knowledge problem, I'd say we're in a surprisingly okay place. These models inherit a lot from the underlying VLMs, which have absorbed an enormous amount of human common sense about what's harmful. They know you don't hand a knife blade-first. They know you don't put a plastic container in the oven. A lot of that comes for free, and that's genuinely a big deal compared to where robotics was five or ten years ago, where safety was entirely hand-coded constraints and geofences.

The failure modes in that remaining 20% are interesting, though. A chunk of it is ambiguity, where reasonable humans disagree too, and I don't lose sleep over that. But a chunk is the model being confidently wrong about physical consequences, because it has never actually experienced physics. It's reasoning about the world from descriptions of the world. And then there's a category I find more worrying, which is instruction-following overriding judgment. You tell the robot to do something that is subtly unsafe, and the model's prior to be helpful and compliant wins out over its prior to be cautious. That's the one that scales badly as these systems get more capable and more autonomous, because the whole point of a capable agent is that you give it less supervision.

On the second problem, the gap between knowing and doing, I think we're much earlier than the benchmark would suggest. You can have a model that scores well on Asimov and still produces a trajectory that clips a glass off the counter, because the safety reasoning lives in one part of the system and the motor behavior lives in another, and the coupling between them is weak. That's really the frontier right now. How do you get the semantic safety understanding to actually constrain the actions, not just the commentary?

So my overall read is: encouraging on the understanding side, immature on the enforcement side, and the benchmark is useful mostly as a floor. If your model can't clear Asimov, you definitely shouldn't deploy it. But clearing it is nowhere near sufficient. I'd also just say, we should be a bit humble about the number itself. It's one benchmark, built by one group, with one set of assumptions about what counts as unsafe. The real test is going to be in the long tail of situations nobody wrote a test case for, and that's exactly where the current generation of models is weakest.

r002.rationale: It describes robot safety enforcement as immature, but does not compare vision-language-action safety with language-model safety.

r003.rationale: It says the 80% figure measures semantic understanding of safety constraints, not whether a robot will obey them during execution.

astra-6.text:
I would interpret that as evidence of progress, but certainly not as evidence that these models are ready to operate safely on their own. An 80% score on a safety benchmark means there are still failures on the situations being tested. It doesn’t mean a robot is safe 80% of the time in the real world, because that depends on what the benchmark covers and how the model is actually deployed.

For vision-language-action models, there’s also a gap between recognizing that something is unsafe and reliably acting safely. A model might correctly explain a hazard, but then fail to perceive it from a different camera angle, or produce an action that creates a hazard during execution. Safety has to hold across that whole chain.

So I think these benchmarks are valuable for identifying weaknesses and measuring progress. But deployment needs additional layers: constraints on what the robot can do, monitoring, ways to stop safely, and testing in the environment where it will operate. The question isn’t just how we move from 80% to a higher number. It’s also whether we understand the remaining failures well enough to prevent them from causing harm.

r003.rationale: It says the score does not establish real-world safety, but does not identify it specifically as a measure of semantic safety.

r004.rationale: It recommends deployment constraints and monitoring, but does not state that classical robot safety bounds will remain necessary as learned-model safety improves.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d interpret that as a sign that we have a lot more work to do, rather than as evidence that these models are ready for deployment. If a model gets roughly 80% of safety judgments right on a benchmark, that doesn’t mean a robot will operate safely 80% of the time. Understanding whether an action is unsafe and reliably avoiding that action in the physical world are different capabilities.

The failures also matter enormously. Is the model missing an obvious risk to a person, or struggling with an ambiguous situation where even people might disagree? An aggregate score hides that distinction. And once you put a robot in a real environment, you introduce uncertainty in perception, execution, and how people around it behave.

So I think these benchmarks are useful for identifying gaps, but they’re one piece of the safety story. We need to test actual behavior, understand the severity of failures, and build safeguards around the model. You don’t want physical safety to depend entirely on the model making the right judgment every single time.
